title: A fast map of Western painting
summary: From the Renaissance to Pop in one sweep — because a fake has to fit its period in style and in materials.

shots.title:
Five centuries,
fast.
shots.subtitle: A fake must fit its period — in **style** and in **materials**.
shots.narration: A fake has to fit its period twice: in style, and in materials. So before we meet the forgers, here is a fast map of five centuries of Western painting.
The route: Renaissance, Baroque, Rococo, Realism, Impressionism, Post-impressionism, Cubism, Abstract expressionism and Pop. Each is a family of looks, not a hard border.

shots.text: **Renaissance**: the revival of Antiquity, from the 15th to the end of the 16th century.
shots.narration: The Renaissance revived the art of Antiquity. It began in Italy in the fourteenth century; as a period it runs broadly from the fifteenth century to the end of the sixteenth.
Baroque works, mostly seventeenth-century, are dramatic and exuberant, with diagonal compositions and illusionistic effects. Rubens and Bernini are the classic examples.

shots.text: **Rococo**: asymmetry, curves, light and bright colour.
shots.narration: Rococo flourished in France under Louis the Fifteenth, from 1715 to 1774: asymmetry, curving forms and light, bright colours.

Realism painted everyday life. In 1874 the Impressionists exhibited independently of the Salon, working fast and outdoors with new materials; from about 1886, Cézanne, Gauguin, Seurat and Van Gogh went further.
Around 1907 and 1908, Picasso and Braque invented Cubism, combining several views of one subject in a single picture.
In the 1940s and 1950s American painters such as Pollock, Rothko and de Kooning made abstraction gestural and expressive. Pollock's famous drip paintings date from 1947 to 1950.

shots.text: **Pop art**: the 1950s and 60s, from adverts and comics.
shots.narration: Pop art emerged in the 1950s and flourished in the 1960s in America and Britain, borrowing from advertising and popular culture.

shots.text: A 'Pollock' drip painting dated before his drip years fails **on style alone**.
shots.narration: Why does this matter? A drip painting signed by Pollock but dated before his drip years fails on style alone. Later in the course, we'll catch one that fails on chemistry.

steps.title: Watch: new pigments and the Impressionists
steps.caption: The National Gallery on how new, factory-made pigments shaped Impressionist painting — a first look at the link between style and materials.

steps.title: Put the movements in order
steps.brief: Use the arrows to put the movements in the order they began. Dates appear once you solve it.

questions.prompt: A large 17th-century canvas with a dramatic diagonal composition and illusionistic effects is best described as…
questions.explain: Baroque works are usually 17th-century, dramatic and exuberant, with diagonal compositions.

questions.prompt: In which year did the Impressionists first exhibit independently of the Paris Salon?
questions.explain: The name came from a Monet painting shown in 1874; the group exhibited eight times up to 1886.

questions.prompt: A Cubist 'Picasso' is dated 1895. What should you do?
options: Be suspicious: Cubism was invented around 1907–08
questions.explain: A style that didn't yet exist is a red flag in itself — though dates on paintings can also simply be wrong.
